1.text:
The chapter begins inside a phrase with no verb in it, "In the Name of Allah", and the grammar is the first thing explained: a verb has to be supplied, and what is supplied is the reader's own act, "I begin" or "I recite", so that this line is not a description of God at all but a way of putting a task inside a claim about Him. Nothing has been asked for, and nothing has been given; the one who begins has only marked where the beginning comes from, and the whole sūrah is placed under that name before a single request is made. Then the two names follow, "the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful", and these are the words the chapter keeps using. Both are drawn from one word for mercy, and that word is employed only when it is He who is being described, which is why the pair is not an honour laid upon Him but a statement of what He is toward what He has made. The first of the two is the wider, used of the vastness of it, a mercy that reaches everything and embraces every living thing; the second is the gentleness in it, the mercy turned toward the one who asks. So the chapter opens on ownership and then on tenderness, and the order belongs to the sense: a reader who begins in the name begins under a description that has already been made gentle. Two further things are settled here before anything else comes. The first is that this line is a verse of the sūrah and not a heading written above it, which is why it is recited aloud and counted, and the second is that the name it uses cannot be given to anyone except Him, since it stands for the essence and not for an attribute among others. The sūrah has asked for nothing yet; the first asking does not come until the sixth verse, and everything between these two names and that request is the reason the opening is so short.

**How to begin a task.**

The best way to begin any task is in the name of God, the Lord, the Being who is the source of all blessings, and whose blessings and mercy are continually pouring upon His creation. To commence any undertaking in His name is to pray that God, in His infinite mercy, should come to one’s assistance and bring one’s work to a successful conclusion. This is man’s acknowledgement of the fact that he is God’s servant, and also brings divine assurance of success.

**A verb is understood.**

So, according to the rules of grammar, some verb is taken to be understood here which should be suitable for the occasion -- e.g., 'I begin or recite with the name of Allah.' Propriety demands that even this verb should be understood to occur after the phrase, so that one does actually begin with the name of Allah and the verb does not precede His name. The preposition 'Ba' has, however, to be placed before the name of Allah, for it is an exigency of the Arabic language. It was to eradicate this practice that the first verse of the Holy Qur'an which the Archangel Jibra'il brought down to the Holy Prophet commanded him to begin the Qur'an with the name of Allah "Read with the name of your Lord." By instructing man to begin everything with the name of Allah, Islam has given to the whole of his life an orientation towards Allah so that he may, with each step he takes, renew his allegiance to the covenant with Allah that nothing he does, not even his very being can come into existence without the will and the help of Allah. But while going to sleep or waking up, the Muslim mentions the name of Allah, renewing his relationship with Him.

**The greatest of the divine names.**

The word, 'Allah' is the greatest and the most comprehensive of the divine names. The word 'Allah' refers to the Essence, and hence this name cannot be given to anyone except Allah. That is why this word has neither a plural nor a dual, for Allah is One and has no associate. It is said that Allah is the Greatest Name of Allah, because it is referred to when describing Allah by the various attributes. Hence, Allah mentioned several of His Names as Attributes for His Name Allah.

**The two names of mercy.**

These last two names of Allah are derived from the Arabic word raḥmah, which means mercy: proving the greatness and vastness of His Mercy and that His Mercy surrounds everything, and embraces all living beings. Every blessing is due to His mercy, and the believers receive the greatest mercy. That is why 'Rahman ' is the exclusive attribute of Allah and the word is employed only when one is referring to Him. The Meaning of Ar-Rahman Ar-Rahim - the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim are two names derived from Ar-Rahmah (the mercy), but Rahman has more meanings that pertain to mercy than Ar-Rahim. Abu Ali Al-Farisi said, Ar-Rahman, which is exclusively for Allah, is a name that encompasses every type of mercy that Allah has. It has been said that name [ism] derives from "brand" [sima]. In other words, he who says "In the name of God" receives that stamp and is marked by that brand. The chapter has only named, and what it names is mercy.

**What else the same passage holds.**

In the Name of God the Compassionate the Merciful There is consensus of all the Muslims on the fact that Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim ‌ ‌ is a verse of the Holy Qur'an, being a part of the Surah al-Naml (The Ant); and there is also an agreement on that this verse is written at the head of every Surah except the Surah al-Taubah . But there is a difference of opinion among the Mujtahids (the authentic scholars who are entitled to express an opinion in such matters) as to whether this verse is an integral part of the Surah al-Fatihah or of all the Surahs or not.

2.text:
"All praise is for Allah" is a statement of ownership before it is a sentence of thanks, and the two cannot be pulled apart here, because the word used for praise carries thanks inside it: what is owed to the one who gives is thanks, and what is given back to Him is praise. The whole of it belongs to Him alone, and the reason given is that every blessing, and every mercy, is His, poured out and sustained, and no one but Him knows their number. Praise is due to the source of a thing, and so this line answers the one before it from the other side: there He was named, here He is thanked. Then "Lord of all worlds" explains why the thanks is total. The word for Lord runs nurture and ownership together, a bringing of a thing on toward what it was made for, by degrees, and it is used of Him with nothing added, which is why it cannot be shared with any of what He has made. The worlds are everything that exists besides Him, the heavens and the earth and what is between them, every living thing and every person, and the same word covers a thousand of them and millions, because the relation is the same in every case: He made, He owns, He nurtures, and none of them is worthy of praise for what it has not given itself. This is why the sūrah begins by teaching a reader what to say first, and what to say about himself afterwards. The two verses of mercy and of judgement sit between this line and the first request, and the praise is repeated in the last third of the chapter, so that the asking in the middle is framed by ownership at both ends.

**Praise and thanks.**

The Meaning of Al-Hamd Abu Jafar bin Jarir said, "The meaning of (Al-Hamdu Lillah) (all praise and thanks be to Allah) is: all thanks are due purely to Allah, alone, not any of the objects that are being worshipped instead of Him, nor any of His creation. All thanks and praise are due to Allah for these favors from beginning to end. " Further, Ibn Jarir commented on the Ayah, (Al-Hamdu Lillah), that it means, "A praise that Allah praised Himself with, indicating to His servants that they too should praise Him, as if Allah had said, Say: All thanks and praise is due to Allah.' It was said that the statement, (All praise and thanks be to Allah), entails praising Allah by mentioning His most beautiful Names and most honorable Attributes. When one proclaims, All thanks are due to Allah,' he will be thanking Him for His favors and bounties. " The Difference between Praise and Thanks Hamd is more general, in that it is a statement of praise for one's characteristics, or for what he has done.

**Three verses of praise, three of request.**

Of these, the first three are in praise of Allah, while the last three contain a request or a prayer on the part of man, which Allah himself has, in His infinite mercy, taught him. The verse in between the two sets has both the features -- there is an aspect of praise, and another of prayer. Thus, the first verse of the Surah, as we said before, combines in itself the praise of Allah and a subtle indication of the first and basic principle of the Islamic creed -- the oneness of God. " (mazhari) The Surah begins with the words Al-hamdulillah, signifying that all praise essentially belongs to Allah.

**The meaning of Lord.**

The next phrase to follow in the Surah speaks of an attribute of Allah -- Lord of the Worlds. The word, Rabb is exclusive to the sacred Being of Allah, and cannot be employed in the case of any created being without adding some qualification, for a created being is itself in need of 'nurture', and cannot nurture anyone else. When it is alone, the word Rabb is used only for Allah. In the Name of God the name of a thing is that by which it can be known. Everything belongs to Him and He is the disposer of their affairs; blessing individuals specifically and humans in general.

**How many worlds.**

So, 'the Lord of all 'the worlds" means that Allah alone gives nurture to all the forms of existents that are to be found in this universe, or in the millions of universes that may lie beyond our own universe in the outer space. According to the well-known commentator Muqatil, the number of worlds is eighty thousand. Seen in the light of this short phrase, 'Lord of the worlds', the universe reveals itself to be an incredibly complex, yet perfectly integrated order. " Al-Qurtubi commented, "This is the correct meaning, that the Alam encompasses everything that Allah created in both worlds. It is also said that this means: the Master of the jinn and human beings. It is also said that (Lord of the worlds) means the Creator of all created beings, their Provider and the One Who changes them from one state into another. When man looks at the world around him, he cannot fail to notice God’s power and mercy abundantly in evidence everywhere. The reader now stands third: the praise is about God, and the one praising is addressed.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The Names of God exalted be He are the archetypal forms ṣuwar nawʿiyya whose specificities and ipseities hūwiyya indicate the attributes of God and His essence and which indicate by their very existence His countenance and by their individuation His oneness. For these are the outward manifestations through which He can be known; Allāh is a name for the divine essence qua essence absolutely without taking into consideration that it may be qualified by the attributes or indeed taking into consideration that it may not be so qualified; the Compassionate is the one who causes existence and perfection to flow upon all things in the measure that divine wisdom requires and to the capacity of the receiving entities qawābil from the outset of their creation; the Merciful al-Raḥīm is the one who bestows the spiritual perfection kamāl maʿnawī that has been earmarked for the human species in the end sc. in the Hereafter.

3.text:
The two names of mercy come again, "the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful", one verse after the sūrah has used them already, and the repetition is the sense rather than a copy left standing. After praise and ownership, the reader has been given nothing new about God, and that is the point: the chapter has stopped twice on the same description, and each time it is the gentle half of it that is repeated. The first of the pair is the wider, used of the vastness of mercy, a mercy that reaches everything and embraces every living thing, and the second is the gentleness in it, turned toward the one who asks, so the two names together carry hope in one direction and encouragement in the other. The position explains the rest. Praise has been claimed, and then ownership in nurture; before the day of requital is named, mercy is named again, so that the warning which follows arrives to a reader who has already been told what He is toward what He has made. It is read this way because a believer's state between these two lines is hope and fear together, and the sūrah does not let either of them have the last word before asking has begun. The recitation of this verse is also a sign of the response it asks for: the name is spoken, the mercy is spoken, and then the servant is ready to be addressed as "You" in the next line, which is where the chapter turns from description to prayer.

**Two adjectives of mercy.**

The Compassionate the Merciful that is to say the One who possesses ‘mercy’ which means to want what is good for those who deserve it. Two names of Allah, Ar-Raḥmān and Ar-Raḥīm, derived from the word raḥmah, or mercy: indicating His mercy for creation, with the believers being the greatest recipients of it. The second verse speaks of the Divine quality of mercy, employing two adjectives Rahman and Rahim of which are hyperbolic terms in Arabic, and respectively connote the superabundance and perfection of Divine mercy. Allah said next, (Ar-Rahman (the Most Gracious), Ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful) We explained these Names in the Basmalah.

**Vivification and light.**

He is the All-Merciful inasmuch as He vivifies, the Ever-Merciful inasmuch as He displays. The vivification is through acts of kindness, the display through lights. He is the All-Merciful who eases the road of wage-earning, the Ever-Merciful who lights up the candle of friendship in the road of the friends.

**Why the line sits here.**

Al-Qurtubi said, "Allah has described Himself by Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim' after saying the Lord of the Alamin', so His statement here includes a warning, and then an encouragement. The reference to this particular attribute in this situation is perhaps intended to be a reminder of the fact that it is not through any external compulsion or inner need or any kind of necessity whatsoever that Allah has assumed the responsibility of nurturing the whole of His creation, but in response to the demand of His own quality of mercy. If this whole universe did not exist, He would suffer no loss; if it does exist, it is no burden to Him. Everything has been extraordinarily and astonishingly adapted to man’s needs. Encouragement and warning in one line, before anything has been asked.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Similarly, Allah said, - (Declare (O Muhammad) unto My servants, that truly, I am the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. And that My torment is indeed the most painful torment.) (15:49-50) Allah said, (Surely, your Lord is swift in retribution, and certainly He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.) (6:165) Hence, Rabb contains a warning while Ar-Rahman Ar-Rahim encourages.

4.text:
"Master of the Day of Judgment" narrows what the verses before it had left open. Praise had been claimed for Him as Lord of every world, and here the ownership is given a day, and the obvious difficulty follows from that: if everything is His at every moment, why is one day named at all. The answer in the sources is that the day is not a limit upon Him but a limit upon the reader, because it is the day when nothing a person possesses, and no relationship they stand in, will be theirs to keep. The word used here covers ownership together with the right to dispose of a thing, and it is used in two readings, one of a king and one of an owner, and both are His: the kingship and the ownership are real here and apparent there, and the reckoning belongs to that day alone. Then the sense of the day is made plain. It is the day of requital, when deeds are weighed out, the good and the evil, and every person is met by what was done, so that the naming of a master is at the same time a warning to whoever is at ease. The mercy of the two verses before has not been withdrawn by this; it is placed beside it, because hope and fear are meant to stand together in the one who recites, and the chapter keeps them in that order. After this line, the reader is able to say "You alone we worship", since no one else has a share in that day, and so the verse is the hinge between what has been described and what will be asked.

**The word for Master.**

The third verse pays homage to Allah as 'the Master of the Day of Judgment or Requital'. The word Malik has been derived from the root, 'milk' which signifies possessing a thing in such a manner that one has the right and power to dispose of it as one likes (See Qamus). So, the phrase 'Master of the Day of Requital' implies total mastery on the Day of Requital. Allah is Al-Malik (King or Owner) Allah is the True Owner (Malik) (of everything and everyone). (Owner of the Day of Judgement) the Arbitrator on the Day of Judgement which is the Day of Reckoning and settlement of disputes between created beings, i.e. the Day when people are judged according to their deeds; there is no judge save Him.

**The reason for naming the day.**

Master of the Day of Judgement that is the day of requite the Day of Resurrection. The reason for the specific mention of the Day of Judgement is that the mastery of none shall appear on that Day except that of God may He be exalted as is indicated by God’s words ‘Whose is the Kingdom today? Allah only mentioned the Day of Recompense here because on that Day, no one except Him will be able to claim ownership of anything whatsoever. For Allah mentioned that He is the Lord of existence, including this earthly life and the Hereafter. Secondly, Allah being the Master, of everything even today as much as on the Day of Requital, why does this verse specifically mentions the Day of Requital?

**The field of action.**

The Day of Requital or the Day of Judgment is the Day appointed by Allah to recompense good or evil deeds. The world is only the fieid of action, the place where one is required to perform one's duty, and not the place for receiving one's reward. On that Day, no one will be allowed to speak without His permission. He is the Master of the day of Judgement, the day in which we will be brought back to life and repaid for what we have done, all of His creation will be held accountable for their actions and recompensed for them. On that day God will ask “To whom belongs the Kingdom today?” [Sūrah Ghafir: 16] No one, no matter how high his status, will answer, and then God will reply Himself, “to God, the One, the Overcomer” [Sūrah Ghafir: 16].

**A warning to man.**

But there is no mention of the thing or things to which this mastery or possession would apply. The phrase 'Master of the Day of Judgment' is a warning to man reeling in his forgetfulness and self-conceit, and an intimation that all his possessions, all his relationships with things and men are only short-lived, and that there shall come a Day when masters will no more be masters and slaves no more slaves, when no one will own anything even in appearance, and the ownership and mastery, apparent as well as real, of the whole universe will be seen to belong to none but Allah, the Exalted. But God's kingship is permanent, today and tomorrow, for it never comes to an end or disappears. Today He is the Lord of the Worlds and tomorrow the Owner of the Day of Doom, and none of the creatures is like this. A day is named rather than the whole of time, and the difference is the verse.

5.text:
"You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help" is the line at which the whole sūrah changes direction, and everything before it was in the third person. Praise, nurture, mercy and the day were spoken about; here the speaker is the one who recites, and God is addressed as You, twice in one sentence, which is why this verse is called the middle of the chapter and the turn in it. The order of the words belongs to the sense. In each half the object stands before the verb, and that order is what makes the "alone" more than an addition: You, and no one else, is what the arrangement carries, so the first half shuts out any partner in worship and the second shuts out any other source of help. Then notice what the two halves are, and what they are not. Worship is the recognition of a thing above the one who does it, with abasement, obedience and love together, and it is the whole of religion gathered into one word; asking for help is the admission that the one who obeys has no strength of their own, and it covers everything a person needs in the affair they have begun. So the first half is the duty and the second is the need, and the duty is put first, so that a reader does not arrive at the asking having forgotten what they came for. The help asked for is left without a purpose attached to it, which is how the request stays open to whatever the day will require. And this verse looks both ways: it answers the four verses before it, which were the praise, and it hands the reader to the one request the chapter makes after it, in the sixth verse.

**What the three verses prepare.**

The fourth verse : “You alone we worship, and from You alone we seek help” has a double aspect, one of praise and another of prayer. The first two verses of the Surah, (All Praise belongs to Allah) and , (the All-Merciful, the Very-Merciful), remind man that, as far as his past and present are concerned, he owes everything to Allah alone, for it is Allah who created him out of nothing, endowed him with the best form in the universe, and with reason and intuition, and continues to sustain and nurture him in the present. The three verses having made it clear that man is totally and absolutely dependent on Allah in all the three states of his life, it logically and naturally leads to the conclusion that Allah alone is worthy of being worshipped, for in Arabic the word ibadah (worship) connotes showing the utmost humility and submissiveness out of an intense respect and love for someone, and such an attitude of willing self-abasement cannot justly be adopted towards anyone except Allah. (You alone we worship) expresses this very natural and logical conclusion.

**The object before the verb.**

The Merit of stating the Object of the Action before the Doer of the Act, and the Merit of these Negations "You...", means, we worship You alone and none else, and rely on You alone and none else. " Allah mentioned, (You we worship) before, (And You we ask for help from), because the objective here is the worship, while Allah's help is the tool to implement this objective. You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help that is to say we reserve worship for You alone by way of acknowledging Your Oneness tawhīd and so on and we ask for Your assistance in worship and in other things. We worship and obey none except You; we associate no one with You, and from You alone do we ask for help in all our affairs.

**Worship and trust.**

And once it has been understood that there is only one Being who can satisfy all our needs, it is equally natural and logical to turn for help in everything to Him alone. It teaches man not to worship anyone except Allah, not to consider anyone else as being really capable of satisfying his needs, and not to beg anyone else to satisfy these needs. Some of the Salaf said, Al-Fatihah is the secret of the Qur'an, while these words are the secret of Al-Fatihah, (5 You we worship, and You we ask for help from.) The first part is a declaration of innocence from Shirk (polytheism), while the second negates having any power or strength, displaying the recognition that all affairs are controlled by Allah alone. This is because after the servant praised and thanked Allah, he stands before Him, addressing Him directly; (You we worship, and You we ask for help from). (Thee (alone) we worship), we turn to you as the only One God and we obey you; ((Thee alone) we ask for help), we ask for your help in worshipping You and from You we obtain confidence in obeying You.

**A request with no purpose attached.**

(to You alone we pray for help) does not mention the purpose for which help is being sought. According to most of the commentators, it generalizes the idea of the request to cover everything from acts of worship to all possible worldly or other-worldly concerns. (Master of the Day of Judgment) tells him that in the future too he will have to depend on Allah alone, for on the Day of Requital one cannot possibly have a helper other than Allah. The first is to adorn the soul through worship and self-purification. The worshiper knows that lordhood is fitting for God and that He is an object of worship without peer, for He is unique and one. I have submitted to You and humbly seek Your help; have mercy on me. And so this line hands the reader to the only request the chapter makes.

6.text:
"Guide us along the Straight Path" is the first thing asked in the sūrah, and the asking is put as a need rather than a possession. The verb carries showing a way, travelling on it, and being made firm there, and the three of them together are what is being requested, so the prayer is not for information about a road but for the staying on it. The sources take the word for guidance in its general sense and its particular one: to be shown the way is given to every creature, and to be led on it to success is what is meant here, and that second degree is the one a person cannot obtain for themselves. Then "the Straight Path" is described by the word used for it, which is a thing set firmly in place, with nothing bent in it and nothing to one side of it; the same word is used of an honest person, so the path and the one walking it are named by one adjective. A road with walls and doors beside it is the image the recitation is given, and the request is to remain inside it, since a person who is not held will deviate, and the path is called great because the one who guides to it has to be asked. What has been asked for is therefore everything at once, at the beginning of a task and at the end of one, which is why this line is the most comprehensive prayer in the book. The worship and the help of the verse before it arrive at their use here: the help is sought for guidance, and guidance is the one thing a servant needs. And the next verse defines the path again, not by rules but by the people who walked it.

**What the request asks for.**

Allah said, (Guide us to the straight path) meaning guide, direct, lead and grant us the correct guidance. Hence, (Guide us to the straight way) means, "Make us firm on the path of guidance and do not allow us to deviate from it." (Guide us to the straight path) guide us to the established Religion that You are pleased with, i.e. It is seeking straightness and firm fixity in the religion.

**The straight path.**

The Meaning of As-Sirat Al-Mustaqim, the Straight Path. As for the meaning of As-Sirat Al-Mustaqim, Imam Abu Jafar At-Tabari said, "The Ummah agreed that Sirat Al-Mustaqim, is the clear path without branches, according to the language of the Arabs. Hence the Arabs would describe the honest person as being straight and the wicked person as being crooked. It is also said that this means: make us firm in holding fast to it. Show and facilitate for us the right way, the path of submission to You which has no crookedness, and make us firm upon it –.

**Showing, travelling, being made firm.**

" These are the three great roots: first showing, then travel ing, then being pulled. " The faithful are saying, "O God, show us Your road, then make us go forth on the road, then take us from traveling to being pulled. " In this verse, the faithful ask for all three of these from God, for not everyone who sees the road travels the road, and not everyone who travels the road reaches the destination. Many there are who hear but do not see, many there are who see but do not recognize, and many there are who recognize but do not find.

**The most comprehensive prayer.**

In other words, Allah Himself, in His great mercy, has taught man what to pray for: “Guide us in the straight path, the path of those on whom You have bestowed Your grace, not of those who have incurred Your wrath, nor of those who have gone astray. To sum up, the Qur'anic prayer (guide us in the straight path) is most comprehensive, and certainly, one of the most important prayers taught to man. No success, no prosperity in this or in the other world can really come without being on the straight path. Particularly so, for man lost in the anxieties of mortal life, the prayer for the straight path is an elixir, though people do not realize it. Lord, show us the path that is, to You, the true path. A prayer for constancy, and the widest petition in the book for the same reason.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Guide us to the straight path that is ‘show us the way to it’. The Prayer for Guidance The last three verses of the Surah consist of a prayer on the part of man. ” The Implications of Guidance A problem of highest significance arises here. The teaching with regard to the prayer for being guided in the straight path is addressed equally to all men or all Muslims and to saints and prophets who have already received guidance and are even a source of guidance for other men. Why should these repeatedly pray for something they already possess? The answer to this question depends on knowing all that is implied by guidance. The answer would, at the same time, remove all difficulties and confusions which arise in the minds of those who, not being familiar with the true signification of guidance, begin to suspect that certain verses of the Holy Qur'an were contradicting certain others. The Meaning of Hidayah or Guidance The best explanation of the word, Hidayah (guidance) has been offered by Imam Raghib al-Isfahani in his Mufradat al-Quran, which can be summed up thus: Hidayah signifies leading someone towards his destination, gently and kindly; while guidance, in the real sense, issues forth from Allah alone, and it has several degrees. The First Degree of Guidance The first degree of guidance is general, and covers everything that exists in the universe -- minerals, plants, animals etc. It would surprise many to hear of guidance in relation to minerals.

7.text:
The path is now defined twice over, and neither definition is a list of beliefs: "the Path of those You have blessed", and then two clauses of exclusion. First the company, which is the way of the people to whom favour and blessings were given, the prophets and those who followed them, so the verse names lives rather than a doctrine, and a reader is asked to want their company. Then the two who are turned away from, and the exclusion is the careful part of the verse, because it is made of two halves that are not the same thing: "not those You are displeased with", and "or those who are astray". The first of those is about people who were given the truth and knew it, and then did not act on it, so the anger named here is earned by a person who had light and walked aside from it; the second is about those who lost the road while meaning well, whose worship is done without knowledge, so that the two are the opposite pairs, knowledge without practice and practice without knowledge. The chapter ends where it began, on a name, an asking, and a company; and the last word of the sūrah is not a threat but a request to be kept from a direction. That is also the reason "amin" comes after it, since the one who recites has just put themselves among people they are asking to be joined to. Nothing further is added here, and the chapter turns back to the prayer and the mercy it opened with, so the whole sūrah stands inside these two lines.

**The path of those blessed.**

the path of those whom You have favoured with guidance from alladhīna together with its relative clause is substituted by ghayri l-maghdūbi ‘alayhim not the path of those against whom there is wrath namely the Jews and nor of those who are astray namely the Christians. (The path of those on whom You have bestowed Your grace). This verse, then, determines the straight path in a positive manner, identifying it with the path followed by men of these four categories. In defining the straight path too, He has also enumerated those of His servants who find special favor with Him -- all of which argues that, in trying to understand the Book of Allah and to act upon it, one cannot solely rely on one's own study and judgment, but must turn to someone who knows. The same path as those of Your creation whom You have blessed with guidance, such as the prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and the righteous ones.

**Those who earned anger.**

The subtle meaning implied by this substitution is that the guided ones are neither the Jews nor the Christians. ” Those who have incurred Allah's wrath are the people, who inspite of being quite familiar with the commandments of Allah willfully go against them out of a calculated perversity or in the service of their desires, or, in other words, who are deficient in obeying divine injunctions. Thus, the essential meaning of the verse is that, in praying for the straight path, we do not ask for the path of those who are the slaves of their desires, perverse in thought and action, and deficient in performing their religious obligations, nor the path of those who are ignorant or unmindful or misled, and indulge in excess and exaggeration in religious matters, but wish for a path between these two extremes, which inclines neither towards excess nor towards deficiency, and which is as free of the promptings of desires as of doubts and confusions and of erroneous beliefs. Keep us away from the path of those who earned Your anger, who knew the truth and did not follow it – as was the case with the Israelites; and keep us away from the path of those who lost their way and were not guided, because they were neglectful in seeking the Truth and being guided by it – as was the case with the Christians. (Not of those who earn Thine anger), not the religion of the Jews who earned Your anger, whom You forsook and whose hearts You did not protect until they became complaisant. (Nor of those who go astray), nor the religion of the Christians who erred from Islam.

**The religion and the people.**

(The path of those whom Thou hast favoured), the Religion of those whom You have blessed with the Religion and who are the followers of Moses, before the blessings of Allah deserted them, in that He shaded them with a white cloud and sent down on them honey and quails when they were in the wilderness. It is also said that (the path of those whom Thou hast favoured) refers to the prophets. Enable us to tread the path of Your chosen servants. Help us to avoid the path of those who have gone astray, and the path of those who have incurred Your wrath due to their obstinacy.

**What the chapter ends on.**

If one associates somebody else with Allah in this respect and, in spite of being familiar with the divine injunctions regarding what is permissible (halal) and what is forbidden (haram), goes against them, believing that someone other than Allah too can demand obedience in these matters, one is virtually worshipping him and being guilty of the sin of association (shirk). O Lord, do not make us be among those whom You have turned over to themselves so that they have been wounded by the sword of separation and fastened by the nail of rejection. Just as You with Your bounty completed their work without them, so also with Your bounty complete our work without us. Amen: thus shall be its custodians; it is also said that Amen means let it be so. But God knows best what is right and to Him is the Return and the final Resort. And so the last line asks for company on a path rather than for a description of one.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Now, to come to the meaning of the 'straight path', it is the path which has no turns and twists. The term signifies the particular way of Faith which equally avoids the two extremes of excess and deficiency. May God bless our master Muhammad his Family and Companions and grant them everlasting peace. One who follows the straight path would, in matters of doctrine and practice both, neither go beyond the limits nor fall short of them. Sufficient is God for us; an excellent Guardian is He. There is no power and no strength save in God the High the Tremendous.
